title: National Association of the Deaf (NAD)
description: The NAD is a civil rights organization for deaf and hard of hearing people in the United States, advocating for equal access in education, employment, healthcare, and technology.

title: American Society for Deaf Children (ASDC)
description: The ASDC is a family-led organization that supports parents and families of deaf and hard of hearing children, promoting ASL and bilingual (ASL/English) approaches so families can communicate fully with their deaf children.

title: Registry of Interpreters for the Deaf (RID)
description: RID sets professional standards for sign language interpreters and works to expand access to qualified interpreting in schools, workplaces, courts, and medical settings.

title: Gallaudet University
description: Gallaudet in Washington, D.C. is the university built for Deaf and hard of hearing students. Instruction happens in ASL and English, and it is a center for Deaf culture, research, and advocacy.

title: National Technical Institute for the Deaf (NTID)
description: NTID is one of the colleges of Rochester Institute of Technology and serves Deaf and hard of hearing students, who study alongside hearing peers with interpreting and captioning support.

title: National Deaf Center
description: The National Deaf Center shares research and resources to help Deaf people succeed in education and employment after high school.

title: Hands & Voices
description: Hands & Voices is a parent-driven organization that supports families of deaf and hard of hearing children, whatever communication approach the family chooses.

title: Hearing Loss Association of America (HLAA)
description: HLAA advocates for and supports people with hearing loss, with resources on captioning, hearing technology, and workplace access.

title: World Federation of the Deaf
description: The World Federation of the Deaf is an international organization of national Deaf associations that works for the human rights of Deaf people and for recognition of sign languages.

title: Video Relay Services (VRS)
description: VRS lets Deaf people make phone calls in ASL through a live video interpreter, who voices the conversation to a hearing person and signs their reply.

title: Captioning and Accessibility Laws
description: Accessibility laws, building on the Americans with Disabilities Act, increasingly call for captions on video and live events, which helps people who are Deaf or hard of hearing.

title: Described and Captioned Media Program (DCMP)
description: The DCMP provides free captioned and described educational media for schools and families.

title: ASL in Schools and Universities
description: A growing number of schools and colleges offer ASL courses and programs, which helps normalize ASL as a full language and grows the number of hearing people who can sign.

title: Learn ASL Online (Lifeprint)
description: Lifeprint offers free online ASL lessons, a sign dictionary, and cultural notes, taught by a long-time ASL instructor.

title: Learn ASL Online (Start ASL)
description: Start ASL offers free online beginner ASL lessons, including vocabulary and practice exercises.

title: Learn the Manual Alphabet
description: Fingerspelling is the best first step. Practice the 26 letters, and use this site's Signs page to see the handshapes. J and Z involve movement.

title: Support Qualified Interpreters
description: Ask for qualified sign language interpreters at public events, school functions, and workplaces, and speak up when an accommodation is missing.

title: Follow and Amplify Deaf Voices
description: Follow Deaf creators, journalists, and advocates and share their work. Awareness works best when Deaf people tell their own stories.

title: Include Captions in Your Own Content
description: Add captions to videos you post and use accessible meeting tools, so Deaf and hard of hearing people can take part.

title: Getting a Deaf Person's Attention
description: Wave, tap a shoulder lightly, or flick the lights. Do not shout, and do not grab or throw things.

title: Talking Through an Interpreter
description: Look at and speak directly to the Deaf person, not the interpreter, and speak at a natural pace. Say "you", not "tell her".

title: Face the Person You Are Talking To
description: Keep your face visible and in good light, do not cover your mouth, and be patient. Writing or typing is fine when you do not sign.

title: Respect Deaf Culture and Identity
description: Many Deaf people see Deafness as a culture and a language community, not a disability to fix. Ask people how they prefer to communicate, and do not assume.
